prompt: Sort each product scenario into price-inelastic demand or price-elastic demand based on how buyers respond to a price change.

cards.text: A pharmacy raises the price of a prescription inhaler by 8 percent, and monthly unit sales barely change.
cards.explanation: Necessities with few substitutes exhibit inelastic demand because buyers continue purchasing almost the same quantity.

cards.text: One brand of sparkling water raises its six-pack price by 15 percent while three rival brands on the same shelf keep their prices unchanged, causing unit sales to drop sharply.
cards.explanation: When close substitutes sit right beside the product, a small price increase causes a large drop in quantity demanded.

cards.text: A commuter bridge increases its morning rush-hour toll by 50 cents, and weekday traffic volume stays at 98 percent of its previous level.
cards.explanation: Commuters have few immediate alternatives during rush hour, so quantity demanded hardly changes.

cards.text: A casual mobile game raises the price of decorative cosmetic skins by 25 percent, and unit purchases fall by 45 percent.
cards.explanation: Percentage change in quantity demanded exceeds the percentage change in price, indicating elastic demand.

cards.text: A grocery store raises the price of table salt from $1.20 to $1.35 a box, and households buy the same number of boxes.
cards.explanation: Household staples that represent a tiny share of the budget and have no close substitutes show inelastic demand.

cards.text: An airline cuts weekend leisure fares to a beach destination by 20 percent, and bookings more than double.
cards.explanation: Discretionary leisure travel responds strongly to price cuts, so demand is elastic.

prompt: Identify whether each business is using good-value pricing, value-added pricing, or a cost-based pricing sequence.

cases.text: A neighborhood supermarket replaces weekly coupon flyers and flash markdowns with consistent everyday low prices across its staple aisles.
cases.explanation: Everyday low pricing (EDLP) is a form of good-value pricing that offers quality and service at a fair everyday price.

cases.text: An independent hotel adds complimentary evening tastings, pillow-menu customization, and late checkout to support a room rate 35 percent above nearby chain hotels.
cases.explanation: Attaching differentiating features and services to support a higher price rather than cutting prices is value-added pricing.

cases.text: An appliance maker engineers a desk lamp, totals the factory and freight expenses, sets a price from that ledger, and then asks sales reps to convince buyers the lamp is worth it.
cases.explanation: Starting with the product and its costs before trying to convince buyers of its value follows the cost-based sequence.

cases.text: A well-known sit-down restaurant launches a counter-service express menu with smaller portions at a lower price point.
cases.explanation: Introducing a less-expensive version of an established brand-name offering is a classic good-value pricing strategy.

cases.text: An auto detailing studio bundles ceramic paint protection, interior steam sanitization, and mobile pickup so it can charge premium rates instead of matching local drive-through wash prices.
cases.explanation: The studio differentiates its offer with added services to justify charging higher prices.

question_text: A kitchenware firm has fixed costs of $180,000, a variable cost of $20 per blender, and a candidate selling price of $50 per blender. What is the break-even volume?
hint: Break-even volume equals Fixed Costs divided by (Price minus Variable Cost per unit).
correct_answer_citation: Week 8: Cost-Based Pricing: Cost-Plus and Break-Even Analysis

options.option_explanation: 3,600 divides fixed costs ($180,000) by the full $50 price, forgetting to subtract the $20 variable cost per unit.
2,571 adds price and variable cost instead of subtracting variable cost from price.
Correct. Each blender contributes $50 minus $20, or $30, toward fixed costs, and $180,000 divided by $30 equals 6,000 units.
9,000 divides fixed costs by the $20 variable cost rather than by the $30 unit contribution margin.

prompt: Sort each launch condition or action into market-skimming pricing or market-penetration pricing.

cards.text: Launching a patented mirrorless camera at a high initial price aimed at professional photographers before lowering the price a year later.
cards.explanation: Setting a high initial price to skim revenue layer by layer from less price-sensitive segments is market-skimming pricing.

cards.text: Entering a price-sensitive consumer cloud-backup market with a $1.99 monthly plan to win a large user base quickly.
cards.explanation: Setting a low initial price to attract a large number of buyers and capture market share quickly is market-penetration pricing.

cards.text: Relying on strong brand prestige and proprietary technology so competitors cannot easily enter and undercut the high initial price.
cards.explanation: Market skimming works only when quality and image support the high price and rivals cannot easily undercut it.

cards.text: Pricing low at launch because unit manufacturing and distribution costs drop steeply once factory volume doubles.
cards.explanation: Falling production and distribution costs at higher volume are a key condition for market-penetration pricing.

cards.text: Accepting a smaller number of early unit sales in exchange for high profit margins on every unit sold.
cards.explanation: Market-skimming pricing makes fewer but more profitable sales from buyers willing to pay the high initial price.

prompt: Which product mix pricing strategy is each company using?

cases.text: A printer maker sells its inkjet printer at a low price and earns most of its margin on proprietary replacement ink cartridges.
cases.explanation: Replacement cartridges must be used with the main printer, making this captive-product pricing.

cases.text: A laptop brand sells a base notebook and lets buyers add a protective sleeve, docking station, or extended warranty at checkout.
cases.explanation: Accessories and extended warranties sold alongside a main item are priced using optional-product pricing.

cases.text: A cookware maker prices its three saucepan tiers at $45, $75, and $120 based on clad-metal thickness and customer evaluations of heat control.
cases.explanation: Setting price steps across items in a line based on cost differences and customer feature evaluations is product line pricing.

cases.text: A water-pitcher company prices the pitcher at $19 and sells required replacement filter cartridges in packs of three.
cases.explanation: The filter cartridges are required to keep using the pitcher, so they are captive products.

cases.text: A climbing gym charges a fixed $25 monthly membership fee plus a $6 usage fee each time a member books a bouldering session.
cases.explanation: Two-part pricing in services (a fixed membership fee plus a variable usage fee) is the service form of captive-product pricing.

prompt: Match each psychological pricing mechanism with the retail scenario that illustrates it.

pairs.term: Price as a signal of quality
pairs.match: A first-time wine buyer who cannot judge vintage quality picks a $38 bottle over a $12 bottle for an important dinner.
pairs.explanation: When buyers lack the information or skill to judge quality directly, they use a higher price as a signal of higher quality.

pairs.term: Placing a standard model beside a luxury model
pairs.match: An espresso-machine brand displays a $1,400 prosumer machine right next to its $450 home model so the $450 price feels reasonable.
pairs.explanation: Placing a standard model next to a luxury model raises the buyer's reference price in the store.

pairs.term: Reference price from remembered past prices
pairs.match: A commuter hesitates to pay $4.50 for a cup of drip coffee because they remember paying $2.75 at the same station last year.
pairs.explanation: Buyers carry remembered past prices in their minds and compare current prices against that internal benchmark.

pairs.match: A luggage tag displays a legitimate manufacturer's suggested price of $240 beside the retailer's selling price of $179.
pairs.explanation: Displaying a legitimate suggested retail price alongside the selling price provides an external reference point.

question_text: In the coffee shopping experiment by Wadi and Ma (2026b), Option A cost $4.99 for 10 ounces ($0.499 per ounce) and Option B cost $5.00 for 11 ounces ($0.455 per ounce), with package weight shown on the detailed product page. When did AI shopping agents reliably choose the better-value $5.00 bag?
hint: Consider how lookup costs and the specificity of the consumer's prompt affected whether the agent inspected the detailed page.
correct_answer_citation: Week 8: How AI Shopping Agents Compare Prices and Unit Costs (Wadi & Ma, 2026b)

options.option_text: Whenever the consumer gave a vague prompt and inspecting the product page carried a lookup cost
options.option_explanation: Under a vague goal and a lookup cost, AI agents frequently skipped checking the package weight and picked the $4.99 bag.

options.option_text: When given a specific cost-minimization goal that prompted them to check the package size and unit price
options.option_explanation: Correct. With a specific cost-minimization goal, AI agents inspected the package weight and selected the $5.00 11-ounce bag with the lower cost per ounce.

options.option_text: Only when Option B lowered its sticker price below $4.99
options.option_explanation: AI agents are not bound by odd-even psychological pricing once they inspect the package size and compute the unit price.

options.option_text: Never, because AI agents cannot divide package price by package weight
options.option_explanation: AI agents can calculate exact unit prices when they inspect all product attributes.
